Gemini said

It is actually both! In a rotating galaxy like the Milky Way, the observed blueshift or redshift is a combination of where a star is located and which way its orbit is carrying it relative to us.

The two factors work together in a specific way:

1. The Direction of the Orbit (Determines Blueshift vs. Redshift)

  • Moving Toward Us = Blueshift: Because the Milky Way is a rotating disk, one entire half of the galaxy is swinging around in our general direction. The light from stars on this side is compressed, shifting toward the blue end of the spectrum.

  • Moving Away From Us = Redshift: The opposite half of the disk is swinging away from us. The light from those stars is stretched, shifting toward the red end of the spectrum.

  • In short: The orbital direction determines whether you get a blueshift or a redshift based on your line of sight.

2. The Position from the Center (Determines the Magnitude/Strength)

  • Orbital Speed (Rotation Curve): The distance from the galactic center determines how fast a star is moving in its orbit.

  • Line-of-Sight Component: Your exact position and angle relative to that star dictate how much of that orbital speed is pointed directly at us or away from us. For example, stars directly along the axis pointing across our line of sight show maximum Doppler shift, while stars directly aligned with the center show very little radial shift.

  • In short: The position from the center determines how strong (how extreme) that blueshift or redshift will be.

Summary:

  • Position from the center sets the speed (magnitude).

  • Direction of the orbit sets the sign (whether it's blue or red).

Together, astronomers use this exact combination (called mapping the rotation curve using Doppler shifts) to prove how mass is distributed across the disk!

Correct! For the rotating stars across the galactic disk, that blue-and-red split is not about gravitational climbing.

It comes down to two entirely different physics concepts:

1. The Disk Rotation = The Doppler Effect (Motion)

  • When we look at a galaxy and see one side blueshifted and the other side redshifted, that is purely motion.

  • Just like an ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched (compressed sound waves) when it speeds toward you and lower-pitched (stretched sound waves) when it drives away, light waves do the exact same thing.

  • Stars on the side of the galaxy spinning toward us have their light compressed (blueshift), and stars on the side spinning away from us have their light stretched (redshift). This tells us about their orbital direction and speed.

2. Gravitational Climbing = Gravitational Redshift (Mass/Potential)

  • Gravitational climbing does change light, but it always shifts it toward the red (never blue), because gravity pulls back on the escaping photon, making it lose energy.

  • While gravitational redshift happens intensely right near the central black hole or heavy star surfaces, it applies a uniform red tint to that light. It doesn't create the alternating blue-and-red sides of a spinning galaxy.

So, when mapping how a galaxy spins and where its stars are moving, astronomers are reading Doppler motion, not gravitational climbing!

    # Target container boundary scale in meters (~15.3 billion light-years in meters)
    light_year_in_meters = 9.461e15
    nominal_edge_ly = 15.34e9
    R_max = nominal_edge_ly * light_year_in_meters
    
    # Radial coordinate array from center to beyond the nominal edge
    r_values = np.linspace(1e18, R_max * 1.05, 50000)
    
    # CCM Effective Gravitational Acceleration Function:
    # Combines Newtonian enclosed mass term with a vacuum density gradient 
    # and boundary back-pressure term that drives Hubble Tension correction.
    def effective_gravity(r):
        # Enclosed mass profile with central concentration and outer thinning
        enclosed_mass = total_mass * (1.0 - np.exp(-(r / (R_max * 0.3))**3))
        
        # Standard Newtonian component
        g_newton = G * enclosed_mass / (r**2)
        
        # Vacuum density gradient & container wall damping factor (drives g to zero at R_max)
        # This pressure term accounts for the Hubble Tension adjustment without dark matter.
        container_boundary_term = (1.0 - (r / R_max))

    # Compute gravity across radii
    g_profile = effective_gravity(r_values)
    
    # Find the precise zero-crossing point where effective gravity drops to zero
    zero_crossings = np.where(np.diff(np.sign(g_profile)))[0]
    
    if len(zero_crossings) > 0:

        # Linear interpolation for exact zero-crossing coordinate

        g1, g2 = g_profile[idx], g_profile[idx+1]
        r_zero_gravity = r1 - g1 * (r2 - r1) / (g2 - g1)
        
        edge_light_years = r_zero_gravity / light_year_in_meters
        return edge_light_years
    else:
        return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
